(a) 
Section 104 is amended by redesignating subsection (c) as paragraph (2) and by inserting after subsection (b) the following new paragraph:

“(c) 

(1) 
Notwithstanding subsections (a) and (b), a report may not be made available under this section to any person nor may any copy thereof be provided under this section to any person except upon a written application by such person stating—

“(A) 
that person’s name, occupation, and address;


“(B) 
the name and address of any other person or organization on whose behalf the inspection or copy is requested; and


“(C) 
that such person is aware of the prohibitions on the obtaining or use of the report.

Any such application shall be made available to the public throughout the period during which the report is made available to the public.”.




 
    (b) 
Section 205(b) is amended by inserting “(1)” after “(b)” and by adding at the end thereof the following new paragraph:


“(2) 
Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a report may not be made available under this section to any person nor may any copy thereof be provided under this section to any person except upon a written application by such person stating—

Any such application shall be made available to the public throughout the period during which the report is made available to the public.”.

fable.w: The section sets conditions for members of the public to inspect or copy reports: a written application stating name, occupation, address, and awareness of use prohibitions. The tempting reading is that the references to "the public" and "application" signal public involvement, but this is only access to records and transparency. No outside party is consulted, heard, or given a right to challenge any federal decision, and there is no rulemaking, hearing, advisory body, or right to sue.
fable.s: a report may not be made available under this section to any person nor may any copy thereof be provided under this section to any person except upon a written application by such person

opus.w: These amendments require anyone who wants to see a disclosure report to submit a written application first, and they make those applications public. The members of the public involved are asking for access to a record, not giving input on a federal decision, so this falls under the application exclusion. The section has no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation, or right to challenge a decision.
opus.s: a report may not be made available under this section to any person nor may any copy thereof be provided under this section to any person except upon a written application by such person stating—
opus.b: **Tempting reading:** Members of the public submit written applications, and those applications are made public. That can look like outsiders interacting formally with the government. **Why it fails:** The application is only a request to inspect or copy a disclosure report. It is a request for access to information, much like applying for a benefit or license. No outside party is consulted or gives input before a federal decision, and no right to sue or object is created.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires individuals to submit a written application to access reports. The definition explicitly states that applications for benefits or grants are not participation. Although this is an application for information access, the act of applying is not a form of consultation or coordination with the government to influence a decision. The subsequent clause making applications available to the public is a transparency measure, not a participatory process where outsiders advise or coordinate with the government.
qwen_chat.s: a report may not be made available under this section to any person nor may any copy thereof be provided under this section to any person except upon a written application by such person stating—
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that making applications "available to the public" constitutes public participation because the public can see who is requesting reports. However, this is merely transparency regarding administrative records, not a mechanism for the public to consult with or influence a federal decision. The core action described is the requirement for an individual to submit an application to access a report.

According to the definition, "It does not include applications for benefits or grants." While this is an application for access to information rather than a benefit, the principle remains: the act of applying for something is not participating in the decision-making process. The public viewing the applications does not involve them in the decision of whether to grant access or how to manage the reports; it is a passive disclosure. There is no consultation, hearing, advisory board with outside members, or right to sue mentioned.
